Leakage through equipment, such as through fittings and values, may also be most prominent with hydrogen because of its smaller particle size, but this can also occur in natural gas and ethane systems. For each of these cryogenic fuels, boil-off gas management is paramount to minimizing supply chain losses and safety risks. If unmanaged, internal pressure can build to dangerous levels and create a substantial risk of boiling liquid expanding vapor explosion (Abbasi and Abbasi 2007). Designated storage and distribution facilities must therefore incorporate adequate pressure relief devices, ventilation systems, and, where appropriate, active vapor management solutions to safely operate. General strategies to minimize boil-off are consistent between LH , LNG, and LE 2 and include enhanced refrigeration, insulation, and reliquefication techniques as well boil-off gas utilization. 4.2.1 Cryogenic Hydrogen Delivery, On-Site-Liquefication, Storage, and Dispensing This subsection details the sources of LH losses through the supply chain from production to 2 end use and provides insights on strategies and technologies that can be leveraged to minimize losses and increase efficiency. We also provide more details on cryogenic hydrogen storage and dispensing technologies. Figure 42 provides a summary of where hydrogen losses can occur throughout the value chain as reported by multiple studies (van Ruijven et al. 2011; Arrigoni and Bravo Diaz 2022; Cooper et al. 2022; Fan et al. 2022; Frazer-Nash Consultancy 2022). Hydrogen losses can be categorized as intentional or unintentional. Intentional losses are operational, such as purging and venting, and are typically done for safety and/or pressure management. Unintentional losses are those such as leakage through equipment or diffusion permeation that occur but are undetected by the operator.
